steps.text: Thread your needle with one strand of 841 and outline the main branch and the bare twig fork with split stitch. Then fill them with long and short stitch, keeping your rows running along the length of the wood - just like the grain of a real branch.

Using 611, blend the shading along the underside of the branch, the little knot stub on the lower left, the tip of the twig fork, and the short leaf stem. Bring your needle up through the 841 you have already stitched so the two browns melt into each other.
Outline the leaf with split stitch in 3013, then fill the outer half with long and short stitch. Angle your rows outwards from the central vein towards the edge, the way a real leaf grows.
Fill the shaded half of the leaf with 989, blending into the lighter green along the central vein. This darker half is what gives the leaf its gentle curl.

Now for the bird! Outline the long tail with split stitch in 799, then fill it with long and short stitch. Keep your stitch direction running from the tail tip down towards the body - tail feathers always flow lengthways.

Using 797, stitch the two long feather shadows inside the tail with rows of split stitch, following the same direction as the 799 beneath. These dark lines are what make the tail read as layered feathers, so keep them nice and crisp.
Fill the small golden patch at the base of the tail with 742 using long and short stitch, angling the rows to follow the curve of the rump.
Just above the golden patch, fill the little olive-green saddle with satin stitch in 936. It is a small area, so keep the stitches short and tidy.

Outline the black back with split stitch in 310, then fill it with long and short stitch flowing from the head down towards the wing. Place your needle just outside the split stitch outline as you fill - this keeps the edge beautifully smooth.

Fill the folded wing with 799, working long and short stitch in gentle curves that fan from the shoulder down towards the wing tip. Don't worry about the dark feather lines yet - stitch right up to their traced edges.
Add the three curved feather edges inside the wing with split stitch rows of 797. Follow the traced curves and let them taper naturally at each end.

Outline the breast and belly with split stitch in 741, then fill with long and short stitch. Curve your rows around the roundness of the chest, from the throat down towards the legs. This bright tangerine is the heart of the whole piece, so take your time and enjoy it!
Stitch the little legs and feet gripping the branch with satin stitch in 3031, keeping the stitches short and following each toe. A few straight stitches on top are fine for the tiniest claws.

Outline the head with split stitch in 809, then fill it with long and short stitch radiating out from the eye - short rows over the crown, longer ones sweeping down to the throat. This is where the bird comes to life, so keep your rows following the curve of the head.
Fill the stout bill with satin stitch in 310, angling the stitches from the base towards the tip. Then, using 169, add the small grey patch at the base of the bill with a few short satin stitches.
Complete the grey band at the base of the bill with 169 - just a few neat vertical satin stitches to soften the join between the bill and the face.

Finally, the eye! Stitch the white eye-ring with tiny split stitches in B5200, then place a plump french knot of 310 (two strands, wound twice) right in the centre for the pupil. That little white ring is what gives your tanager its bright, curious gaze. Your Darwin's Tanager is complete - give yourself a big pat on the back!
